title: Check yourself: Workflow or agent: the distinction and the first three patterns

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A support bot runs three model calls in one order, wired together by the application's code. How does the article classify it?

options.text: An agent, because the model decides each next step in a loop
options.says: Ruled out because agents "are typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop", and here the program, not the model, sets the order.

options.text: A router, because a classifier hands the input to a specialist
options.says: Ruled out because "Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task", while in this bot no step picks which task follows.

options.text: A sectioning pattern, because independent subtasks run side by side
options.says: Ruled out because sectioning is "Breaking a task into independent subtasks run in parallel", while these three calls run one after another.

options.text: A workflow, because the sequence is fixed before the first request
options.says: The page says "Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths."

questions.stem: A product team wants an assistant that answers questions from a small document set, and is weighing a multi-agent design. What does the article recommend as the starting point?

options.text: A single model call that adds retrieval and examples
options.says: The page says "optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough".

options.text: A routing workflow with one specialist prompt for each topic
options.says: Ruled out because a workflow is also an agentic system, and the page says to find "the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed".

options.text: A framework whose layers hide the prompts and the replies
options.says: Ruled out because frameworks "often create extra layers of abstraction that can obscure the underlying prompts and responses".

options.text: An agent that plans its own search steps in a loop
options.says: Ruled out because the article reserves agents for "open-ended problems where it's difficult or impossible to predict the required number of steps".

questions.stem: A moderation service must check a user message and also draft a reply at the same time. The two jobs do not depend on each other. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Voting, where the same prompt is run several times for a majority
options.says: Ruled out because "Running the same task multiple times to get diverse outputs" is voting, and these are two different jobs.

options.text: Prompt chaining, where each call processes the output of the previous one
options.says: Ruled out because chaining is for steps "where each LLM call processes the output of the previous one", and these jobs do not depend on each other.

options.text: Sectioning, where separate subtasks run side by side and are joined
options.says: The page says sectioning is "Breaking a task into independent subtasks run in parallel", with a guardrail beside the answer as its example.

options.text: Routing, where a classifier picks one specialized path for the input
options.says: Ruled out because "Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task", and here both jobs run.
